items.title: Sunday Reboot: Unhinged robots and commentator curses
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, iPhone Duo robots may change the reviewing process, and Murphy's Law is alive and well when anyone talks about tech CEOs.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

Unhinged reviews

It's been a few weeks since the first reviews of the iPhone Duo came out. However, while the opinions of the reviews are one thing, there's another thing that is far more interesting.

There's been so much focus on the hinge that it's eclipsing pretty much everything else about the smartphone. To be fair, it's the headline feature, and so it's going to draw a lot of attention.

That attention hasn't been great, exactly. Since launch, we've been plagued by social media posts of a mystery screen break seemingly caused by a weak component in the hinge mechanism.

We've also seen one component maker threaten legal action for unqualified accusatory opinions.

But when it comes to the hinge in a reviewing sense, some outlets decided to do things differently. No bombastic damage-fueled videos, but instead checking that the hinge will work for the lifetime of the device.

Not by using it for a long time, though. More by performing as many actuations of that hinge as possible.

This week, CNET revealed the details of the iPhone Duo's endurance test on a custom rig that opens and closes the smartphone. After over 440,000 folds, the display was still unfolding, with the hinge getting about 95% of the way open.

That's well over the number of times you would expect to open and close the iPhone Duo if you owned it for ten years.

It's not the only outlet to attempt something like this. Joanna Stern's New Things did something similar, attaching a motorized rig to the iPhone Duo. Running at 17 folds per minute, it achieved over 32,000 folds across four nights with "no noticeable deterioration."

This is all activity that goes beyond the usual routine for a review. Even bigger outlets with the funding and the knowledge base for destruction testing don't bother to go down this route of inquiry.

To be fair, it's borderline consumer testing at this stage.

It does, however, raise a question that affects me. Since things like Stern's relatively minimal test rig exist, should other publications consider doing similar electronic projects to do similar repetitive testing when the product hype allows it?

Am I going to have to learn basic electronics and work out how to code something for an Arduino? Do I have to get the 3D printer up and running for something other than plastic desk figurines and replicas of guns from Destiny 2?

I don't think I need to do that just yet. But if the reviewing industry is going to continue this sort of testing, it'll be another thing to invest my spare time into learning.

Goddamnit, Jensen

Readers may be aware of the Sunday Reboot posted two weeks ago that took aim at OpenAI's Sam Altman. His commentary about how your Mac's RAM was wasting away when it should be used by AI companies was not taken that well.

It turns out that when you put a CEO's feet to the flames, they can sometimes feel it.

Altman tried to perform damage control, renaming himself temporarily to "Ram Altman" on X and declaring that he had argued for a ramp-up of memory production for a "long time."

It's a response from the OpenAI chief that is a bit flippant, but really the only healer here is time. Or at least, the gradual failure of human memory.

However, AI CEO foot-in-mouth recovery aside, that column also included something that should be addressed this week. Namely that somehow I have been afflicted by the Commentator's Curse.

Early on in the piece, I discuss how CEO pronouncements can go wrong, due to being made by out-of-touch rich people. That point still stands in general, though.

The problem is that I pointed to the relatively sane comments made by Nvidia's Jensen Huang about paying a billionaire's tax. He was OK with handing over the cash, which is certainly the opposite of what others had said.

At the time, Jensen seemed like a CEO who was relatively normal. Sure, he had a shiny jacket like he was cosplaying someone from The Matrix, but he didn't appear to have any massively weird beliefs, or at least didn't express them in public.

Alas, that was not to last. Almost as if the universe decided my comments wouldn't go unpunished, Jensen was suddenly accused of having an affair with a person accused of being a Chinese spy.

Just for good measure, it wasn't the only affair, either. Embroiled in a massive scandal, Huang was then forced to resign in disgrace.

It's not the end of things for him, either, as he now faces scrutiny by the U.S. government over the whole Chinese spy thing. It also leaves his legacy at Nvidia tainted, as the company seeks to stabilize the ship.

At the very least, he gets to spend the rest of his life with massive wealth and the hope that the glare from the media dies down at some point.

The shortlist of "CEOs who seem normal and haven't done anything doolally yet" is now a bit shorter.

I'm now watching John Ternus as one of the last on the list, quietly hoping there aren't any skeletons in that Apple-shaped closet.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed Apple's cursing challenges, as well as how the new Apple Watch Live Rewind and Siri Recaps being a step towards an episode of "Black Mirror."

items.title: Apple TV+ 'Slow Horses' faces the glue factory after eight seasons
items.content_html:
Fans of the Apple TV+ thriller "Slow Horses" may not continue past season 8, because it will have caught up with the book series.

Apple confirmed back in September that there would be an eighth season of the Emmy and BAFTA Award-winning spy drama "Slow Horses." However, it seems improbable that it will continue beyond that season for a long time, if at all.

Speaking to The Times, Olivia Cooke said "I am shooting the last season." Cooke, who plays "Sid Baker" on the show, added "never say never" about the warning, since it's what she was told.

The show felt like it was ending, with a "melancholy, distracted" cast and crew seemingly mourning the show's end.

Apple hasn't confirmed it will be the last season, or if there will be future episodes on the way.

Last legs?

The problem "Slow Horses" faces is one involving source material.

Season eight will be adapting "Clown Town" from the "Slough House" book series by Mick Herron. That book was released in 2025, and is the most recent in the series, meaning there's nothing newer to base the show on.

Herron has said there is an intention to continue the story with more books. But, since books can take a long time to write and get published, that can be a long time.

Apple could go down the route of "Game of Thrones" and have the show's story branch off from the books. Though, based on the reaction of fans, that didn't go down well at all.

There's also the possibility of resting the show until more books are available. Though a pause can also be taken as an opportunity by Apple to end the adaptation completely.

Mercifully, there's still some time before fans have to deal with the possible end of the show. Apple TV+ started streaming season six of the show in September, with season 7 probably arriving in 2027.

items.title: Face ID & telephoto lens are coming to iPhone Duo, eventually
items.content_html:
While the timetable isn't clear, Apple is reportedly working on adding Face ID to the iPhone Duo. However, the effective engineering deadline for the late 2027 refresh is coming soon, and the feature may not make the cut.

Apple reportedly has two main priorities for the second-generation iPhone Duo. Those are, sensibly, adding Face ID, and adding an Action Button. We've spoken about the Action Button before, and the most likely implementation is a combination with the camera control button.

But, the loudest complaints we've heard about the model is about the lack of Face ID. A report on Sunday morning by Mark Gurman claims that prototypes exist with Face ID, with integration into having the VCSEL for the biometrics on the outer display.

The hardware, codenamed V78, is nearing the final design stages before first prototypes are assembled and test production starts. As such, Gurman claims that Apple is running out of time for proper integration and inclusion in the 2027 update to the device.

Other goals for future generations include a telephoto camera lens, and reducing the thickness and weight of the unit. He also notes that customer feedback about it, other than what Apple already had on its roadmap that overlaps, shouldn't be expected until the iPhone Duo 3.

items.title: Lightweight Apple Glasses rumored for WWDC 2027 reveal
items.content_html:
Apple could finally announce its smart glasses during WWDC 2027 with privacy-focused features built around the Secure Exclave and Siri AI.

Apple's smart glasses, which AppleInsider has previously dubbed Apple Glass or Apple Vision, have been rumored for years. With the latest products like Apple Watch and HomeView being built around Secure Exclave technology, the pitch for smart glasses is coming into focus.

According to the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, Apple is expected to announce the Siri AI-powered smart glasses during WWDC 2027. They would launch later in the year.

Current prototypes of the smart glasses have oval lenses with cameras flush to the frame. Also, a proprietary magnetic connector on the left arm lets testers use the glasses easily while charging.

It isn't clear if charging while in use will be a feature at launch. The frames are reportedly thinner than Meta's current offering as well.

Expect more on Apple's smart glasses strategy as we approach WWDC 2027 in June. That timetable isn't set in stone, but it is allegedly the current goal.

Apple's Vision

It has become increasingly clear that Apple wants to preserve its privacy image even as it announces AI products that watch, listen, and report on the world around you. The Secure Exclave is central to that feature set and messaging.

Live Rewind is a controversial feature that doesn't record any audio to provide a transcript

On Apple Watch, the Secure Exclave is used for Audio Intelligence features like Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Those tools never actually "capture" or "record" audio in the traditional sense, but analyze data from environment audio to power the features.

The Secure Exclave is a processing unit separate from the main system and nothing can be extracted from it, even by hacking into the main CPU. No audio files are saved or recoverable, thus Apple is able to get around the legal definition of "recording." Though, that hasn't been tested in court just yet.

Apple's HomeView also uses a Secure Exclave for processing audio and video feeds. The device authenticates the user based on visible users in the field of the camera and the voice recognition in the environment.

Like on Apple Watch, no audio or video is recorded, just referenced by the AI tools for authentication purposes. However, Apple's complex system still allows the camera to be used for FaceTime calls through special permission structures.

Visual data from AirPods or Apple smart glasses could appear in Siri Recaps

All of this makes perfect sense for Apple's smart glasses strategy. The company will likely lean in hard on not making "pervert glasses," which is the nickname given to Meta's Ray-Ban glasses that have been the center of so much abuse.

Google's Android XR glasses line will face similar problems. They appear to have similar functionality to Meta's glasses with minimal promises to privacy preservation.

With Samsung's upcoming line of smart glasses, users are able to capture video and photos with the glasses, but a recording light will be visible and allegedly can't be covered or removed. It remains to be seen if these privacy protections and promises not to train on user AI visual data will be enough.

Apple's approach, on the other hand, already has years of groundwork laid around provable privacy and security features found on iPhone. Also, by announcing Audio Intelligence on Apple Watch and the authentication features in Apple HomeVeiw first, Apple is preparing the market for the camera glasses that are somehow different from the much maligned pervert glasses.

AirPods with Cameras are expected to arrive ahead of Apple's smart glasses with a similar feature set.

It isn't yet known if Apple intends to let users capture video, audio, or photos from their version of smart glasses or camera-equipped AirPods. If I were Apple, I would pitch them as cameras for AI, not the user, and the perfectly good iPhone camera in your pocket will do the trick for capturing a moment.

Hindsight is 20/20

The newsletter is fairly confident in its information on the potential release and strategy around Apple smart glasses. However, it's history of reporting around the Apple Vision team has been spotty at best.

Apple Vision Pro and its development continue in spite of poor reporting on the product

Much of this report can be arrived at through simple conjecture based on Apple's previous strategies and already-announced features. The WWDC 2027 announcement date is new, though a second-half of 2027 launch window isn't.

There were several months where the publication reported that Apple's smart glasses are due in late 2026. Then suddenly, that shifted to late 2027 to align with other reports, though it cited internal struggles as usual.

The publication blames Apple's Siri AI launch delays and development snags, but that doesn't explain why everyone else had the currently agreed upon late 2027 release window. The publication has also run into repeated errors when reporting on Apple Vision Pro moves.

As with all rumors, it is best to remain skeptical.

items.title: Siri AI will be how Apple Glass will unseat Meta's smart glasses
items.content_html:
Apple's plan for its AI-equipped smart glasses is to lean on integrations with a user's existing iPhone apps, in a similar way to the CarPlay-like HomeView.

Apple's long-rumored smart glasses are expected to lean on AI processing for its first release. However, the way that it functions with AI will be key to their success.

Writing in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Mark Gurman says Apple is expecting app developers to prepare for the eventual introduction of its smart glasses in 2027.

However, rather than having apps running fully on the glasses, Apple wants developers to focus on Siri integrations. The aim is for specific functions within apps to be accessible to Siri, which can then be called upon by users wearing the glasses.

This is an approach that is similar to the rollout of HomeView. That device does not allow third-party apps to run directly, but it does let apps with existing CarPlay support to play audio and video.

For a device like smart glasses, this makes a lot of sense, especially if Apple keeps to its plan of making thin and light smart spectacles. It won't have enough onboard processing available to handle much in the way of apps.

That's something CarPlay and Siri AI solve by pushing the hard work to a nearby iPhone.

Winning through Siri AI

Apple's vision for the smart glasses will include Apple making a similar plea to developers to work on those elements before the launch of the Apple Vision Pro.

This push to use Siri AI is being performed with Apple believing it has the upper hand on current market dominator Meta. While Meta is entrenched in smart glasses, Apple's advantage comes from its pool of developers.

With a much larger pool of developers at its disposal in the App Store, as well as having worked on Siri integrations for the iPhone long beforehand, there should be little effort needed to make those Siri integrations work with the smart glasses.

With any luck, it should launch with a robust and vast number of things you can call upon Siri to do, without waiting for developers to catch up. All because the work had already been done.

items.title: Apple Glasses will not have Apple Vision Pro-style augmented reality
items.content_html:
Apple Glasses will not have Apple Vision Pro-style augmented reality

A report saying that Apple is preparing a new Apple Glasses type of headset, also says that they will not be like a lighter Apple Vision Pro.

In the short term, the expectation is that Apple will release its rumored AirPods update featuring sensors and cameras to register the environment around the wearer. Then Bloomberg says that those plus unspecified further sensors will be included in the glasses.

Reportedly, Apple employees are even referring to the glasses as "AirPods for your face." In the devices' first generation, these glasses will not present any visual data to the wearer.

So there'll be no in-vision data and no in-vision apps. What they will have is greater battery life than AirPods.

It's claimed that the battery life will be such that users can wear the Apple Glasses all day without recharging. Then, too, it should be easier for people to wear glasses in terms of comfort.

Such glasses should also be more acceptable in company than AirPods.

While there won't be any apps actually running on the Apple Glasses, there will be Siri AI. As well as responding to spoken commands, Siri AI in the glasses will be constantly receiving environmental information from the sensors.

Cameras and sensors

This report follows a recent supplier leak that appeared to confirm that Apple was working on both Apple Glasses and AirPods with cameras. It's still the case, though, that these cameras will not take photos.

Instead, they will provide sensors for AI and accessibility use. It's likely to be similar to how Siri Recap works now on the Apple Watch.

Rather than recording images, the cameras could provide data that is analyzed by Siri AI in real time. It sounds just like the way that Siri Recap does not record audio, yet is able to provide summaries of conversations.

So, perhaps, the cameras in Apple Glasses could detect an obstruction and Siri AI could verbally warn the wearer. That's already possible with an iPhone, since accessibility features such as door detection were added with iOS 16 back in 2022.

items.title: Crime blotter: Truck driver pleads guilty to theft of iPhones, iPads
items.content_html:
An accused thief jumped into a lake after an AirTag found his location; the man accused in a sex sting is not Apple's head of PR; and an assault at a U.K. Apple Store, all in this week's Apple Crime Blotter.

The latest in an occasional AppleInsider, looking at the world of Apple-related crime.

Truck driver pleads guilty to theft of iPhones, iPads from shipment

Draterrius McCollough, a 31-year-old truck driver, has pleaded guilty to federal charges. He was accused of stealing more than 200 items from shipments, worth $30,000, including "numerous" iPhones and iPads.

According to the Justice Department, he resides in Alabama, worked for a transportation company, and drove shipments from "a major American retailer's warehouse" to stores throughout Louisiana.

The company's fraud investigations team noticed in January that large amounts of items had gone missing and traced them to McCollough. A search of his Baton Rouge apartment discovered the iPhones, iPads, and other stolen items.

Investigations also found that he had stolen a "brand-new Apple iPhone 17 Pro Max" from a shipment just days before the raid.

When he was arrested in February, WAFB identified the retailer as Walmart and his employer as FedEx. The shipments crossed state lines, which is why the case is federal.

AirTag used to track car theft suspect who jumped in a lake

Police used an AirTag to track a stolen car in Seattle, ultimately locating it during a pursuit that ended when the suspect jumped into Lake Washington.

According to KIRO, it happened on October 30, when the suspect stole an SUV from a driveway while the victim was unloading the car. The owner used an AirTag to track where the car was going and notified police, who located the car with the suspect in it.

Then, police said, the suspect reversed the car, hit the patrol car and a nearby home. The suspect got out of the car, pointed a gun at officers, dropped the gun, and jumped into the lake.

After treading water for 25 minutes, during which he told officers he had outstanding warrants, he eventually swam to shore. Not before spitting out a white substance that was identified as fentanyl.

He was arrested for "stealing the SUV, felony assault, and unlawfully possessing a firearm due to being a convicted felon."

Man arrested in amateur sex sting falsely claimed he worked for Apple

A 34-year-old California man was caught in early November by a "child predator hunter" social media team, trying to meet what he thought was a 15-year-old boy at a Ritz-Carlton hotel in New York. He was later arrested by the NYPD.

The New York Post reports the social media posts had falsely identified the man as an "Apple PR ops exec" and "the head of PR for Apple."

The man has not actually worked for Apple, although according to the Post, he had falsely claimed on LinkedIn to have been an employee of the company.

The Post reported that he had worked for "a third-party outside vendor that the tech giant used to book travel arrangements."

Man arrested for assault at U.K. Apple Store

Police in Kent, in the U.K., arrested a man in October for an alleged assault at the Apple Store at the Bluewater shopping center in Kent.

According to ITV, the man "allegedly made inappropriate comments towards a woman, pulled her hair and touched her lower back over her clothing."

The 36-year-old was arrested on suspicion of assault.

AirTag used to discover stolen stones

In what's certainly an only-in-the-U.K. story, a councilor in Lancashire used an AirTag to solve the theft of 300-year-old coping stones.

The Lancashire Post writes that 30 stones went missing from the 18th-century wall connecting the towns of Holmeswood and Rufford.

After some of the stones were taken, parish councilor Matt Smith placed an AirTag in a loose stone, betting thieves would take that one too.

The plan worked, and police arrested a 41-year-old man after finding the stones in his backyard. He received a 12-month sentence, suspended for 22 months.

iPad stolen from parking lot at NFL game

On October 26, the Philadelphia Eagles lost to their hated rival, the Dallas Cowboys, on Monday Night Football. For one fan, the night got even worse when an iPad was reported stolen from a car at Lincoln Financial Field.

According to the Citizen app, Philadelphia Police received a report that the iPad was taken from a Cadillac at the stadium on game day. The iPad was later tracked to a location on Haverford Avenue.

Thief caught putting iPad down his pants

A man in Australia was caught on camera stealing an iPad from a massage parlor, stuffing the iPad down his pants, and fleeing the business.

The Advertiser reports the man's actions were captured on CCTV.

"Please stay vigilant, keep an eye on your reception areas and don't leave valuables unattended," the business said in a Facebook post, along with the video.

Doctor's office employee reports Apple gift card scam

On November 2, a doctor's office employee visited the New Lenox police department in Illinois to report a scam. They received text messages from someone claiming to be their boss, asking them to purchase an Apple gift card for $200 and send the information.

According to Patch, the person did as they were told, but later realized the messages were not genuine and they had been scammed.

AirTag used to recover stolen toolbox in Florida

A stolen toolbox was recovered in West Palm Beach, Fla., after an AirTag in the toolbox led police to the man accused of stealing it.

CBS 12 explains the owner had left the toolbox in his truck before entering a Taco Bell. The accused thief was spotted taking the toolbox, leaving it behind a dumpster, and then also entering the Taco Bell.

Later, the suspect was seen retrieving the toolbox and putting it in a different car.

When police tracked the toolbox to the suspect's residence, the suspect told them he "found it in a store he was renovating after homeless people had been removed, and that someone put it in his truck."

Four MacBooks and an iPhone stolen from Kenyan podcasters

A popular podcast in Kenya, the Mic Cheque Podcast, had gear stolen from their tour bus during a stop at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (JKUAT).

According to Pulse, the stolen items included three MacBook Pros, a MacBook Air, an iPhone 13, two pairs of headphones, and eight solid-state drives.

items.title: Siri AI has arrived on 2021 and newer Apple TV 4K models

Apple has released tvOS 26.2.1, and has updated an article on its support site listing the requirements for Siri AI on the set-top box.

According to Apple, Siri AI will be available via tvOS 27.2.1 on Apple TV 4K from the second generation onward. It also requires a paired Siri AI-enabled device nearby.

While Apple rolled out the 27.2.1 updates for iOS, macOS, watchOS, and others earlier in the week, tvOS was notably absent. However, given what we've learned about Siri AI support coming, it makes sense that Apple may have held off on the rollout.

And late on Friday, tvOS 27.2.1 arrived, adding the feature.

Apple's new Apple TV 4K is showing up on customers' doorsteps on Friday as well. AppleInsider has reviewed it, noting that it's a considerable upgrade that comes at considerable cost.

items.title: After more than 10 years worth of folding, the iPhone Duo still works
items.content_html:
As it turns out, you can damage your iPhone Duo by opening and closing it too much, at least theoretically. Don't worry, you don't have that much time on your hands.

Three weeks ago, CNET put the iPhone Duo on it's custom testing rig, the Fold-A-Phone. Now, after 440,300 folds, it's finally reached its breaking point.

Sort of, if you're willing to define "breaking point" loosely.

According to CNET, it still opens 90 to 95 percent of the way on the Fold-a-Phone rig. And if you open it by hand, you can still get it to open fully; it just doesn't feel as snappy as it used to.

CNET's readings and footage showed changes in how much force it took to open the phone around 390,000 folds. This included losing the distinctive snap it had upon opening it fully, and the hinge, perhaps unsurprisingly, was looser.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

The display still holds at other angles without issue. The lack of flatness does not meet CNET's criteria for failure, which would need to include loss of power, sensors failing to detect the screen where it needs to be within the given timeframe, or screen blackout.

As CNET points out, at 100 folds per day, 440,300 folds represents about 12 years of use, which is long past the practical lifespan of the iPhone Duo. CNET plans to continue testing the iPhone Duo.

Initial reviews and reactions around the PROLED MacBook Pros, iMac, and iPad mini are in, plus there is plenty more to discuss around living with the iPhone Duo. Your hosts cover these topics plus more on Apple AI on the AppleInsider Podcast.

The touchscreen has proven to be the least interesting part of Apple's updated MacBook Pro models. They're thinner, lighter, and sport a tandem OLED display that is finally on par with the iPad Pro.

Reactions to the iPad mini have been mixed given the existence of the iPhone Duo. For those that don't have Apple's foldable, it will continue to prove to be the best tablet-as-a-tablet Apple makes.

Wesley has published his iPhone Duo photography overview and shares more of his thoughts on the camera system. William has encountered more Siri annoyances, but there's a chance they could be fixed in iOS 27.3, or perhaps iOS 27.4.

items.title: 100,000 iPhone Duo apps is a start, but there's a long way to go
items.content_html:
Apple recently announced that over 100,000 apps have been built for the iPhone Duo, but with developers working with multiple SDKs, it could still be a long time before your favorite apps really make full use of what the first foldable iPhone has to offer.

At first blush, that 100,000 figure certainly grabs the attention, especially just a few weeks after launch. But it doesn't tell the whole story, and there's still work to be done.

While Apple's big number applies to apps that have been built from scratch or refactored to fully support the iPhone Duo, many more haven't. Yet more find themselves in some kind of middle ground.

Those apps don't look terrible on an iPhone Duo, but they don't look as great as they could. For that, some work will be needed.

That's the key here, because there is no guarantee that will happen anytime soon. Depending on who or which company makes the app in question, it might never happen at all.

In reality, apps in the App Store were split into three categories with the release of the iPhone Duo. To truly understand how that impacts iPhone buyers, we first have to get into what those categories actually are.

When you open an app on your iPhone Duo, there are three possible outcomes.

What to expect

When you open an app on your iPhone Duo, there are three possible outcomes.

Best-case scenario

If you're using one of those 100,000 apps Apple lauded in its press release, you'll get the best possible experience. The app will completely fill both the inner and outer displays, edge-to-edge.

The updated Google Maps uses the whole of the inner and outer displays on the iPhone Duo.

You'll also notice that the app features adaptive vertical navigation bars. The controls that would normally be on the bottom of the display now reside on the side, well within one-handed thumb reach. If you're right-handed, of course.

Apps like this are also built with Apple's Split View feature in mind, and are fully compliant. They'll work as expected when you use your iPhone Duo to multitask.

Most likely to happen

The second possibility is the middle ground. And while not quite as impressive as the best-case scenario, it's more than usable.

These apps resize to fill most of the iPhone Duo's inner display, but there are no vertical navigation controls to be found. The same also applies to the outer display, so the already squat display will be more cramped.

In fact, you'll get a big black vertical bar where the status bar lives on the right side of the display. The full width of the display won't be used as it would in the best-case scenario.

A terrible experience

The third possibility is one that users of older apps will likely be faced with. From my testing, it also affects apps from bigger companies.

Unfortunately, these companies are those less likely to rush to update their apps to make the most of the iPhone Duo. Especially considering its relatively small user base when compared to the rest of the iPhone lineup.

In use, an iPhone app like this appears full-screen on the outer display, just as it would on a traditional iPhone. But the navigation bar will remain in its usual position and not on the right side.

When the iPhone Duo is opened, you'll get something akin to using an old iPhone app on an iPad. That is, you'll see a small app in the middle of the display surrounded by large black borders.

Why this happens is all down to how, and when, the app was built.

The SDK trap

Apple gave app developers the tools they needed to make great iPhone Duo apps as soon as it was announced. The first Xcode 27.1 beta with iPhone Duo support was released on September 18, 2026, a little over a month before it went on sale.

Apps built using this too, against the iOS 27.1 SDK, are the ones that fare best. These are the apps built for iPhone Duo, and they make up the 100,000 Apple mentioned previously.

As has historically been the case, these tend to be apps from independent developers. But some big-name companies have gotten in on the act, some even before the iPhone Duo went on sale.

Apps built against the slightly older iOS 27 SDK make up that second section, the most likely home for your favorite app. These apps are certainly usable, but they don't offer the best experience that they could.

However, those apps are incredible improvements over apps built with pre-iOS 27 SDKs. Those are the ones that have no idea the iPhone Duo exists and look terrible as a result.

Apps that haven't been updated in months, and especially if it's been years, fall into this category. So do apps that have been updated but still use an old SDK, including some big ones.

Two that spring to mind immediately are the PlayStation and Xbox apps. Amazingly, the Nintendo app is a third.

Another notable app not to be updated to even fill the iPhone Duo display is Football Manager 27. That's despite the fact that it's a brand-new title at the center of a recent Apple Arcade press release.

A brand-new game that's being heavily publicized by Apple Arcade, yet no iPhone Duo support

I live in the UK, and the NHS app falls foul of this issue. A fact I'm reminded of every time I book an appointment with my doctor or order a prescription.

There are countless more, and the worrying thing is that these are apps that may stay this way for far too long. The people behind the NHS app probably aren't rushing to add iPhone Duo support, after all.

Support is not full support

There isn't much anyone can do about legacy apps, or those from developers not inclined to update them for the iPhone Duo. It's frustrating, but it isn't the only issue here.

The apps in that middle ground should also be a focus, and it's important that we don't allow developers to rest on their laurels. Apps filling the iPhone Duo's display shouldn't be the benchmark.

Instead, I think it's important that everyone remembers that apps can be better. Apps like Apple's 100,000 that make full use of the iPhone Duo's inner display, reworked navigation bar and all.

If developers are allowed to do the bare minimum and we settle for that middle ground, we risk another Apple Vision Pro situation.

Just as iPad apps work on Apple's headsets, apps built against the iOS 27 SDK also work on the iPhone Duo. But neither makes the most of what those two devices offer over anything else.

If the foldable iPhone is going to be the success the Apple Vision Pro isn't, it'll need great-looking apps along the way.

items.title: Designing HomeView was a hard but fun journey, says Apple
items.content_html:
Apple executives have revealed that the new HomeView is the culmination of years of design effort balancing audio, privacy, and especially Siri AI.

As the first buyers take delivery of the new HomeView, two of Apple's executives involved have been discussing the device. Speaking to TechRadar, they describe developing HomeView as a difficult but rewarding journey because of where it is meant to be used.

"Home life is super busy, you know, it's complicated, it's complex, and people are moving around," said Matthew Costello, Apple's Vice President of Hardware Engineering, "and we wanted a device that was really designed specifically for that environment."

Cecilia Dantas, Home Product Marketing, said that the overall goal was to "give you exactly what you need in the moment." She added that it was vital that HomeView "do that with absolute simplicity."

Dantas says the plan was always that each person's data be available to them, but privately. "It comes from your iPhone," she said. "If you leave, [if] you take your iPhone with you, it goes with you, and it's not kept on the device at all."

It's not intended to be just about calendars and reminders, though. Dantas says that she uses a shared family album on her HomeView, and it updates as others add to it.

HomeView can display photos on its screen when not in use.

"I'm really proud of the moments of connection that it brings," she said. "It is delightful to see the photos come up."

Long development

Costello said that ultimately HomeView "really was constructed around Siri." He said that Apple wanted to tie Siri AI into a "device that is communal in nature in a home."

"We thought [that] was a really important moment," he said. "Together with our Design Studio, we went on a long journey of exploration to figure out 'how do you create something that's a unique form for the home?'"

Despite Siri AI software being central to the design, the development actually started with the display. The company wanted a shape that "was unique from other form factors we have inside of Apple."

"So we ended up with the aspect ratio you see today," he continued. "That then drove a lot of decisions around where things were placed."

Learning from the HomePod

Chief amongst the components that had to be arranged within that form factor were the HomePod-like speakers. But it wasn't just a case of where they could fit, because the HomeView comes in two very different versions.

"Getting the display right with the audio, and then the split-audio architecture between having the sort of higher-frequency speakers in the head," said Costello about the main screen, "and then the lower-frequency woofer in the base was something we worked through."

"How do you then extend that to the wall-mounted version as well?" he asked. "It was a really fun, hard-fought journey to get to where we ended up."

HomeView's gets personialized information, such as calendar events, from your iPhone.

Beyond the speakers, though, Apple says that great attention was paid to the display. "I really love the fact that this is the lowest light performance we've ever engineered into a product," said Costello, "it's down to 0.3 nits."

"So officially, I represent the most dim product ever inside of Apple," he continued. "I don't know if that's a good or bad thing, but I'm super-happy about that."

Alongside the development of the hardware, Costello said that "we really custom-built this user interface for the home, so the apps and experiences that matter in the home setting are really front and center."

HomeView first reactions

AppleInsider's Andrew O'Hara agrees enough with Costello and Dantas that he says he wants to buy five HomeViews. But at the same time, he's found that it is obviously a first-generation device, and that it has clear faults alongside its equally clear potential.
